cues.text: We close this study session with a final consolidation.
Think of it as a checklist of what you should be able to explain, in your own words, before you move on.
I'll go through each item in order, and for each one I'll tell you what you should be able to do.
First, know the four industrial revolutions.
The idea is that industry has changed in major steps, and each step was driven by a new source of power or a new way of organising production.
The first is usually linked to mechanisation, using water and steam power to drive machines.
The second is linked to electricity and mass production, with work divided into repeated steps on a production line.
The third is linked to electronics and information technology, which brought programmable automation.
The fourth is Industry 4.0, where physical machines are connected to digital systems, sensors, data and networks.
When you revise, be able to name each revolution, say what technology or capability defined it, and explain how it changed the way work was done.
Use the exact wording in your session notes for the details of each stage.
Second, know the Industry 4.0 design principles.
A design principle is a guiding rule for how a connected system should be built.
The principles in your notes describe what a smart, connected production system should be able to do.

Typical themes include machines and systems that can communicate with one another, virtual copies of physical processes, decisions made closer to where work happens, information available in real time, and systems built from parts that can be added or changed.
Check these against your session notes and be ready to state each principle and explain it with a simple example.
Third, know the enabling technologies.
These are the tools that make Industry 4.0 possible.
They include sensors and the Internet of Things, which gather data, and networks and cloud computing, which move and store it.
They also include analytics, artificial intelligence and automation, which turn the data into decisions and actions.
For each technology, be able to say what it does, what problem it solves, and how it depends on the others.
Sensors without analytics only produce unused data, and analytics without good data has nothing to work with.
Fourth, know the Internet of Things architecture.
Architecture means the layers of a system and how they connect.
In simple terms, the system starts with devices and sensors that sense the physical world.
It continues with connectivity that carries the data, then processing and storage where the data is handled, and finally applications where people or other systems use the results.
Be able to walk through the layers in order, say what each one does, and explain what happens if one layer fails.
Fifth, understand the feedback in cyber-physical systems.
A cyber-physical system joins a physical process to computing.
It works as a loop.
Sensors measure what is happening, software analyses it and decides, and an actuator or a person acts on the physical world.
The change is then measured again.
This loop is the feedback.
Be able to describe it step by step, and explain why the closed loop is what makes the system responsive rather than merely informative.
Sixth, understand the trade-offs between edge and cloud.
Edge computing means processing data close to where it is produced, such as on or near the machine.
Cloud computing means processing it in remote, shared data centres.
Processing at the edge is generally faster to respond and keeps working when the connection is weak.
The cloud generally offers more storage and computing power and can combine data from many sites.
Neither is simply better.
Be able to explain when a task needs a fast local reaction and when it benefits from large-scale analysis, and why many systems use both.
Seventh, know the smart factory applications.
A smart factory is a production site that applies these technologies so that machines, products and systems share data and adjust their work.
Be able to describe the applications in your notes, say what data each one uses, and say what benefit it aims to deliver.
Eighth, know predictive maintenance.
Maintenance can be reactive, meaning you repair after a breakdown.
It can be scheduled, meaning you service at fixed intervals.
Or it can be predictive, meaning sensor data is used to estimate when a fault is likely, so you act just before it occurs.
Be able to explain the data flow from sensor to analysis to maintenance action, and the reasoning for why this can reduce unplanned downtime.
Treat any specific savings figures as examples only, unless your notes present them as evidence.
Ninth, know the risks.
Connecting machines and data creates exposure.
Be able to explain the risks listed in your notes, such as cybersecurity, data protection, reliance on connectivity, cost and skills.
For each risk, be ready to state what could go wrong and what response your notes suggest.
Tenth, know the digital leadership theories.
Technology does not transform an organisation by itself.
Leaders set direction, shape culture, and guide people through change.
Be able to name each theory in your notes, say in your own words what it claims about how leaders should behave, and apply it to a case about introducing new technology.
Finally, know the measurable outcomes.
A transformation should be judged by results, not by how much technology was bought.
Be able to state the outcomes and key performance indicators from your notes, and explain how each one would be measured and what it tells a manager.

A good check for yourself is to take one smart factory idea and trace it through the whole list: which revolution it belongs to, which principles and technologies it uses, how the data flows, where the risks are, how leadership drives it, and how you would measure success.
If you can do that, you have consolidated the session.
